chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He said: 'Any man who startles another man from a wall, or dislodges him from his animal, so he falls and dies, then he is liable for his blood money; and if he breaks something, then he is liable for the blood money of whatever is broken from him.'

key_terms.انْكَسَرَ: he broke (a limb or part of the body)
key_terms.نَفَّرَ: to dislodge or cause to fall off

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on liability for injuring someone by startling them?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of *daman* (financial liability) in Shia jurisprudence, establishing that direct causation (*sababiyyah*) through startling (*tafzīʿ*) incurs full responsibility for blood money (*diyah*) or compensation for injury. It highlights the juristic consensus on holding the initiator accountable for the immediate physical consequences of their action, whether death or fracture, reflecting the broader legal theory of *al-ḍamān bi-al-sabab* (liability via cause).

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al Halby, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Whichever man panics a man from the wall, or dislodges him from his animal, so he falls off and dies, so he is responsible for his wergild; and if he (the rider) breaks something, so he is responsible of the wergild of whatever has been broken from him’.
